title: How To Show Hospitality When You Live in a Small Home
author: Tim Challies
summary: Prompted by reader questions after an earlier article on downsizing housing expectations, Tim Challies offers practical, tested advice for practicing hospitality in a small home, drawn from over twenty years hosting from a roughly 1,200-square-foot townhouse. The eight tips move from mindset (don't be ashamed of your house; treat guests with respect rather than trying to impress them) to logistics (buy an extendable table, avoid high-end furniture that makes overflow seating stressful, designate at least one guest-sleeping space, enlist nearby friends to host overflow as 'a community project'). Challies frames the discomfort of close quarters — disrupted routines, being woken early or kept up late — not as a hospitality failure to be engineered away but as part of the point, citing 1 Peter 4:9's instruction to 'show hospitality to one another without grumbling.' The piece closes on a theological reframe that undergirds the whole essay: the home was never really the owner's to withhold, but the Lord's, entrusted to be used well — meaning a small home limits the scale of hospitality but must never become an excuse to abandon it.
points: Challies's most transferable practical tip is the extendable table (seating six normally, up to 12 in a pinch) paired with deliberately low-to-mid-range furniture, since expensive furniture makes the inevitable overflow seating and spills of real hospitality stressful rather than relaxed.

He reframes the discomfort of hosting in tight quarters — disrupted sleep, awkward moments, limited privacy — as substantively part of hospitality's purpose rather than a logistics failure to be minimized, grounding this in 1 Peter 4:9's command to host 'without grumbling.'

The 'ask nearby friends to host the overflow' tip turns hospitality's physical limits into a communal rather than individual project, widening who's responsible for welcoming guests beyond the homeowner alone.

The closing theological move — that the home was never the owner's to withhold but the Lord's, merely entrusted to them — reframes hospitality as stewardship obligation rather than optional generosity, regardless of house size.
quotes: Housing in my area and many others has gotten far more expensive over the years, and I have known many people who have become "house poor" by continually upsizing. Yet my family and many others can attest that it is possible to live contentedly in a relatively small home.
Just the other day we had 10 people for dinner, which means the table stretched from the wall of the dining room all the way into the living room. It was tight, but that's okay. We're used to it.
We understood this to be the Lord's provision for us and never wanted to be ashamed of what he provided.
When you have more guests than your home can hold, ask nearby friends whether they can host the overflow. There's no reason that hospitality can't become a community project!

No one ever said hospitality would be easy and, in fact, I'm quite sure that the difficulty is part of the point of it. There's a reason that Peter says "show hospitality to one another without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9).
It is not actually your home, but the Lord's. He has simply entrusted it to you and now holds you responsible for using it well.
A small home may limit some of the ways you do this, but it must not prevent you from doing so altogether.
